nodes.question: How did Schmidt et al. (2004a, b) and Schulte et al. (2021) evaluate bio-based insulation materials?
nodes.answer: They conducted a cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) and compared the materials using thermal resistance as the functional unit while investigating all environmental impacts as prescribed in International Organization for Standardization (1997).
nodes.paragraph: Standard construction practices are still reliant on products made from fossil-based resources, especially for insulation materials. Insulation materials manufactured from bio-based resources have emerged as an alternative to the more tradi- tional fossil-based insulations. Bio-based insulations have the advantage of using renewable resources, if produced under environment-friendly practices, can store carbon (Lawrence et al. 2013) and, if not recyclable, can sometimes be used for soil conditioning (Beigbeder et al. 2019). Several studies have found lower environmental impacts for some bio-based material (Schmidt et al. 2004a; Murphy and Norton 2008; Pargana et al. 2014; Schulte et al. 2021; Carcassi et al. 2022). Schmidt et al. (2004a, b) and Schulte et al. (2021) compared the environmental impact of plant- based insulation materials to conventional materials. Both Schmidt et al. (2004a, b) and Schulte et al. (2021) performed a cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) and compared the materials using thermal resistance as the functional unit. Products were compared by investigating all the environ- mental impacts prescribed in International Standard Organi- zation (1997).

nodes.answer: The LCA considered eleven newly commercially available bio-based insulation materials.
nodes.paragraph: The dynamic LCIA in Carcassi et al. ( 2022 ) and Hawkins et al. ( 2021 ) demonstrated the significant potential of bio-based insulation to offset carbon emissions. Whilst both Carcassi et al. (2022) and Hawk - ins et al. (2021) demonstrated the advantages of bio-based materials, they based their work on specific products, using EPDs for Hawkins et al. (2021) and developing a Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) for a small-scale material production in Carcassi et al. (2022). Their investigation is therefore lim- ited to specific contexts. In this study the investigation of the environmental impacts is based on a case study in which the construction site is based in the UK, but it not limited to specific manu- facturer locations, and products. Product variations (density and thermal conductivity) were considered in the LCA of eleven newly commercially available bio-based insulation materials. nodes.question: What was the outcome of the developed scenarios and dynamic LCIA in the project?
nodes.answer: The scenarios and dynamic LCIA provided a range of data for each environmental impact and material, helping professionals make informed design decisions.
nodes.paragraph: Follow - ing EN 15804 (2012) + A2(2019), modules A and C were considered. Module D was excluded as information and data on burdens and benefits of bio-based materials are not well defined. The materials were compared using a common thermal transmittance as the functional unit. Scenarios that combine variations in material properties, transportation and end-of-life phases were developed, providing a range of data for each environmental impact and each material. Ranges were used to rank and investigate the environmental impacts. Results were also used as an input for dynamic LCIA to investigate the influence of biogenic carbon and the poten- tial benefits of temporary carbon storage. The project aims to provide environmental impact of bio-based materials not based on a specific product, and a single point result, but on a comprehensive and more generalised dataset. By providing a range of data through scenarios and dynamic LCIA, pro- fessional would be able to make informed design decision. 2 Materials and methods Eleven new, commercially available bio-based materials (mycelium, flax, sheep wool, cellulose, wood fibre, cork, hemp lime, hemp fibre, polylactic acid (PLA), recycled cot- ton and recycled wood board) were selected and compared to two common insulation materials (PUR.

nodes.question: What is the significance of using the LCA perspective in the study?
nodes.answer: The LCA (Life Cycle Assessment) perspective serves as the backbone for making recommendations regarding the evaluation of environmental impacts of EHDs.
nodes.paragraph: There is no one-size-fits-all solution to mitigate the envi- ronmental burden of EHDs. Solutions such as eco-design strategies, replacing single-use with reusable EHDs, circu- lar economy strategies, and proper treatment and disposal could enhance the overall sustainability of the healthcare industry. However, the perceived environmental benefits of these strategies are not yet fully understood, nor is the effect on environmental sustainability when considering direct and indirect impacts. To address the above-mentioned shortcom- ings, this study focuses on two objectives: (1) to investi- gate the current state of knowledge on the evaluation of the environmental sustainability of EHDs and (2) to identify research gaps in environmental impact evaluation studies and make recommendations using LCA perspective as the backbone. 2 Methodology This section starts with a brief description of the search strategy used to identify and select eligible studies on the environmental sustainability assessment of EHDs. Subse- quently, the method for extracting data and analysing infor - mation from the selected studies is described. 2.1 Literature search strategy The literature search followed a structured procedure involv - ing the following steps: (i) identifying the databases and search terms, (ii) screening articles, (iii) categorising the selected articles, and (iv) synthesising and analysing the articles.

We compare the antibacterial material with a non-antibacterial control and perform a life cycle assessment (LCA) based on ISO 14040 [ 7] and ISO 14044 [ 8]. Based on the results, we infer the possible directions for further development of the AgNP-HH-PLA biocomposite. nodes.question: Why is up-to-date data important for conducting Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)?
nodes.answer: Up-to-date data is crucial for conducting LCA as it reflects real changes in the environmental impacts of industrial activities over time.

As the The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment environmental impacts of industrial activities evolve rapidly over time, the availability of up-to-date data is crucial for conducting LCA that reflects real changes (Teh et al. 2020; Carri res et al. 2021). Furthermore, databases often appear inconsistent with each other due to different development approaches, thus raising problems of comparability between the different analyses performed (Zhang et al. 2020; Sica et al. 2022). In this framework, the use of digital technologies (DTs) is emerging as a valuable solution to improve the Life Cycle Inventory phase (Ingrao et al. 2021; Sica et al. 2022; Yang et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2024). They include tools such as cloud computing, blockchain, big data analytics, and simulation (Bai et al. 2020 ). nodes.question: What does LCA guarantee in terms of evaluation processes?
nodes.answer: LCA guarantees rigor and uniformity in calculations, helping with the comparability of results and transparency in evaluation processes.
nodes.paragraph: 2019; Beylot et al. 2020; Schulz et al. 2020). As LCA is a standardised methodology, it guarantees rigour and uniformity in the calculations of environmental impacts, helping comparability of results and transparency in evaluation processes (Hellweg and Mil i Canals 2014). By delivering comprehensive quantitative insights, LCA supports the evaluation of alternative production pathways, fostering transitions from linear to circular systems and assessing the potential consequences of adopting alterna- tive productions (Prado et al. 2017; Br ndstr m and Saidani 2022; Sica et al. 2022). While a product may exhibit high circularity performance, this does not necessarily lead to a reduction in environmental impacts (Pe a et al. 2021; Roos Lindgreen et al. 2021). Therefore, LCA provides a scientific and methodological basis for measuring the environmental performance of products and processes within the circular economy, supporting more informed decision-making pro- cesses (Serenella et al. 2015; Byrne et al. 2017; Cordella et al. 2020). Like- wise, Bj rnbet and Vild sen S (2021) study on a Norwegian manufacturer revealed that LCA is a suitable methodology for the development of circular business models as it pro- vides quantified results about the environmental impacts of circular strategies, limiting the risk of problem shifting and considering multiple environmental impact categories. nodes.question: What recommendation is made for improving impact assessment estimates in LCA studies?
nodes.answer: LCA studies should uniformly include SOC changes and be conducted over longer timespans to fully assess the stability of added C storage.
nodes.paragraph: 2022 ), SOC accumulation is expected to hold a major potential to mitigate agricultural GHG emissions (Petersen et al. 2013 ). To improve impact assessment estimates, LCA studies should therefore uni- formly include SOC changes and be conducted over longer timespans to assess the stability of added C storage for a full accounting of agricultural GHG emissions (e.g. including beef production) (Cusack et al. 2021). Goglio et al. (2015) reviewed different methods to account for SOC in agricultural LCA. In their ranking of preferences of SOC estimation methods, models were pre- ferred to measurements. Due to inherently high spatial vari- ability of SOC stocks and the high cost of measurements, there is little measured data available from the case studies to allow for the assessment of changes in SOC (Heikkinen et al. 2021). Conversely, different modelling approaches are already widely applied to assess changes in SOC in agricul- ture and have been shown to generate accurate results (e.g., Riggers et al. 2019; Jebari et al. 2021). nodes.question: What are the two computational stages of LCA where uncertainties in carbon footprint estimates can arise?
nodes.answer: The two computational stages are life cycle inventory analysis (LCI) and life cycle impact assessment (LCIA).
nodes.paragraph: 2020). Additionally, there is now a consensus that LCA stud- ies must acknowledge uncertainties inherent within pro- duction systems to ensure their scientific robustness (lgos et al. 2019). Theoretically speaking, uncertainties in carbon footprint estimates can arise from either of the two compu- tational stages of LCA, namely, life cycle inventory analysis (LCI) and life cycle impact assessment (LCIA). Within the context of livestock production systems, however, the choice of LCIA methodology has been shown to impart negligible effects on global warming potential as long as the timescale of analysis (e.g. 20 years, 100 years, or 500 years) is clearly defined (Reckmann 2013). Uncertainties associated with LCI, on the other hand, have considerable impacts on envi- ronmental footprints arising from different farming systems (McAuliffe et al. 2017) and are also of relevance to a large population of practitioners around the world.
